b: One thing we knew ahead of the announcement of the new James Bond: whether it was Robert Pattinson or Callum Turner or Idris Elba or Jack Lowden or Josh O’Connor or somebody only six people had heard of, there would be an immediate hue and cry from some corners of the Internet. (There’s never a “hue” without a “cry.”)

When Pattinson got the nod, the backlash centered on him being too famous, too young, too pretty, not handsome enough, the fact he’s already starred in massive franchises, his acting style, and if you dig deep enough, somebody probably had an issue with the names he’s given to his dogs over the years. (For the record: Patty, Solo, Bernie and Bear. What an outrage!)

This is the Gilded Age of Casting Controversies. Remember the ludicrous outrage over certain casting choices in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” with vocal critics moaning about “historical inaccuracies” in an ancient oral mythic poem filled with sea monsters and gods? How about the blowback against a new version of “Harry Potter,” which had the temerity to cast the talented Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape?

We never learn from Hollywood history. When Sergio Leone wanted to cast Henry Fonda as a cold-blooded villain in “Once Upon a Time in the West” (1968), even Fonda wondered if he was the right choice, given his record of playing mostly principled and even heroic characters. Mary Tyler Moore in “Ordinary People” (1980), Michael Keaton as “Batman” (1989), Heath Ledger in “The Dark Knight,” even Daniel Craig as James Bond—all of these casting decisions were criticized before we actually saw the work and realized a perfect choice had been made.

Not that I’m immune to such prejudices. It’s not as if I thought in advance that Bryan Cranston—Tim Whatley from “Seinfeld” and the lovable dad from “Malcolm in the Middle”—would create arguably the most memorable anti-hero-turned-full-villain in television history in Walter White on “Breaking Bad.” Or what about Selena Gomez joining comedic legends Martin Short and Steve Martin for “Only Murders in the Building”? Was I surprised that Gomez proved to be a formidable third lead, absolutely nailing the role? Maybe just a little.
Anyone who tells you they know for certain how Pattinson will play as Bond is bluffing. As always, the proof is in the final print—but there’s reason for optimism on a number of fronts.

Of course, the argument about physical attractiveness is subjective, and Pattinson has spent much of his post-“Twilight” career playing against his looks in service of character work (even in leading-man roles). Still, we know he can pull off the dashing, globe-trotting, intelligence operative persona, as evidenced by his work as Neil in “Tenet.” The character is practically a test drive for Bond, with Pattinson wearing bespoke suits, delivering his lines with dry wit and keeping his cool in the hottest moments.

The age question is actually a selling point. Bond is roughly 35-42 years old in the Ian Fleming novels. Pattinson is 40. George Lazenby was 29, Sean Connery was 31, Craig was 37, Timothy Dalton was 40, Pierce Brosnan (who co-starred with Pattinson in “Remember Me”) was 41, and Roger Moore was 44 when they were cast as Bond.

By far the biggest factor in Pattinson’s favor is that he’s a versatile actor who has consistently delivered interesting, provocative work across a vast spectrum. Look no further than his performance in another storied franchise as Bruce Wayne/Batman.

Where the billionaire Bruce Wayne has historically been portrayed as a suave, womanizing smooth-talker who commands the room, Pattinson teamed up with director Matt Reeves (who co-wrote the screenplay for “The Batman” with Peter Craig) to flip the script and give us a Batman who was actually more comfortable in the costume. This Bruce Wayne was a socially awkward eccentric.

From “Good Time” (2017) to “High Life” (2018) to “The Lighthouse” (2019), Pattinson has done what all good actors do: he makes us forget who he is and believe in his character. Look at his insanely creative work in Bong Joon-ho’s “Mickey 17,” where he played multiple versions of the same character and created distinct personalities.

With Pattinson’s “Dune: Part Three” director Denis Villeneuve helming the new Bond movie and a script from Steven Knight (“Eastern Promises,” “Locke,” “Peaky Blinders”), and one of the best actors of his generation in the lead, perhaps we should take a breath and consider this could be the beginning of an exciting new chapter for 007.
